About the maker

Clay found me in a cold little studio — and never let go

[Placeholder biography — the maker's own story will sit here.] Ember & Earth began at a borrowed wheel in a garden studio, with more cracked pots than keepers. Years on, the ritual is the same: wedging the clay at dawn, throwing while the kettle boils, and opening the kiln like it's Christmas morning.

Everything is made slowly and in small firings, using stoneware clay and glazes mixed in the studio — ash, iron and mineral tones pulled from the landscape outside the door. The aim is simple: honest, everyday pieces that make an ordinary Tuesday breakfast feel a little more considered.

Stoneware clay, fired to 1,280°C for strength
Glazes mixed by hand in the studio
Seconds sold at studio sales — nothing wasted
Commissions welcome for weddings & cafés
— The Maker, Ember & Earth

The craft

How my ceramics are made

From a bag of raw clay to a finished piece takes three to four weeks, four pairs of hands' worth of patience — all from the same two hands.

Step one

Hand-building

Vases and sculptural pieces begin as coils and slabs, pinched and joined by hand. Finger marks are left where they fall — proof a person made this.

Step two

Wheel-throwing

Mugs and bowls are thrown on the wheel, centred by feel as much as by eye, then trimmed at leather-hard stage and fitted with pulled handles.

Step three

Glazing

After a first bisque firing, each piece is dipped, poured or brushed with studio-mixed glazes — layered so colours pool, break and blush over edges.

Step four

Firing

The glaze firing climbs to 1,280°C over twelve hours, then cools for two days before the kiln is opened. Some pieces sing. A few don't — those never leave the studio.
